summary: A report of an IAB workshop held in March 1997 at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, New Jersey. Participants identified the core security components of the Internet architecture, listed documents that needed to be written, and agreed that security must not be optional.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2316 records a workshop held by the IAB in 1997 about security in the Internet. It lists which security mechanisms the group considered core, what was still missing, and what every protocol author should write about threats.

why did the iab say security is not optional

subtitle: A 1997 workshop report that argued security must be designed in, not bolted on.

tldr.problem: Attacks on the Internet were increasing, and many protocols had security sections that said little or nothing, so the IAB wanted a security architecture and guidance for protocol designers.
tldr.mechanism: Twenty-four attendees met at Bell Labs on 3 to 5 March 1997, picked the protocols they considered core, named the pieces that were missing, chose the documents to write, and drafted guidelines for the Security Considerations section of an RFC.
tldr.outcome: The report is Informational. Its main conclusion is that security is not optional and has to be designed in from the beginning.

facts.value: Bell Labs, Murray Hill, New Jersey

today: RFC 2316 is an Informational workshop report from April 1998, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the views of one workshop and defines no protocol.

sections.title: Why the IAB Held the Workshop
sections.content:
On 3 to 5 March 1997 the IAB held a security architecture workshop at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, New Jersey. The ultimate goal was to design a security architecture for the Internet. More concretely, the group wanted to understand what security tools and protocols exist or are being developed, where each is useful, and where adequate security tools are missing. They also wanted to provide useful guidance to protocol designers: to get rid of the phrase security issues are not discussed in this memo from future RFCs, guidance on acceptable analyses was needed.

There were twenty-four attendees, listed in Appendix A. The report notes that the overwhelming majority used some form of cryptography when connecting back to their home site from the meeting room, but that the situation on the rest of the Internet was not nearly as good, because few people use encryption even when they should.

The reason for the workshop was that the rate of attacks is increasing. Apart from the usual few elite hackers who find the new holes, many canned exploit scripts are around, and attackers have got smarter: rather than going after random university machines, more and more target the Internet infrastructure, such as routers and high-level name servers. The problem is compounded by organizational laziness, because users and system administrators want magic security, meaning whatever they do is secure regardless of whether it is, or even can be.
sections.plainLanguage: Attacks on the Internet were getting more frequent and more organised, and most protocols said nothing useful about security. The IAB brought twenty-four people together for three days to work out what to do about it.

sections.title: General Philosophy and the IETF's Structure
sections.content:
The group concluded that in general end-to-end security is better, so one should use something like PGP or S/MIME for email rather than relying on an IPsec layer. Relying on the security of the infrastructure is a bad idea, because it too is under attack, and even firewall-protected intranets can be subverted. At best, the report says, the infrastructure should provide availability, and it is the responsibility of individual protocols not to make unreasonable demands on the infrastructure during an attack.

The IETF's own structure compounds the problem. By intent it is a volunteer organization, so nobody can be ordered to do security work. The report asks who should do it: the other protocol designers, who often have neither the time nor the interest nor the training to do it, or the security area members, who might not be interested in some subject area or lack the time themselves. The answer is that the IETF cannot order them to serve.

To the extent that the IETF does have management, it is embodied in the working group charters, which are in essence contracts between the IESG and a working group spelling out what is to be done and on what schedule. The report asks whether the IESG can unilaterally impose new requirements on existing working groups, and what happens if security cannot be added without substantial changes to the fundamental structure of a protocol that has been reworked over several years. There is also a perception problem: that IPsec will somehow solve the security problem. The report says it will not, and cannot, because although IPsec provides excellent protection of packets in transit, it is hard to deploy on individual hosts, does not protect objects that may be retransmitted such as email messages, does not address authorization issues and cannot block against excess resource consumption.
sections.plainLanguage: The message to protocol authors is that the ends should protect themselves, because the middle of the network cannot be trusted. The message to the IETF is that volunteers cannot be ordered to add security to protocols they do not care about, so it has to be written into their terms of work.

sections.title: Guidelines for Security Considerations
sections.content:
The report starts from a definition. A threat is, by definition, a vulnerability available to a motivated and capable adversary. CERT advisories are quite predictable given a knowledge of the target, so they represent an existence proof, but not a threat analysis. The point is to determine what attacks are possible, that is, the capabilities of a potential attacker, and to formulate a defence against them, or to argue convincingly that the attack is not realistic in some environment and to restrict use of the protocol to that environment.

The recommended guidelines are written as requirements on every RFC. All RFCs MUST meaningfully address security in the protocol or procedure they specify, and MUST consider that they are giving their data to the enemy and asking it to be delivered to their friends and used in the manner intended. Consideration must be given to the ramifications of the inherent danger of the situation. Each document MUST do due diligence to list the threats to which the protocol is vulnerable; the use of the legal term does not imply legal liability, but rather the level of responsibility expected to be applied to the analysis. That discussion might occur throughout the document or in the Security Considerations section, and if it occurs throughout it must be summarized and referenced in the Security Considerations section.

Each document MUST then discuss which of those threats are ameliorated by protocol mechanisms, such as the SYN attack being ameliorated by clever code that drops sessions randomly when under SYN attack; which are ameliorated by reliance on external mechanisms, such as TCP data confidentiality provided by IPsec ESP; which are irrelevant; and which are not addressed by the protocol, which results in an applicability statement saying that the protocol should not be used in an environment subject to this attack.

The workshop also chose several documents to write: a taxonomy of attacks, because in order to defend a protocol one must know the kinds of attacks that are possible; implementation hints and pitfalls, because even a sound protocol can be subverted by an improper implementation; an examination of firewall issues, because firewalls are both a common defence and a much-reviled wart that are unlikely to go away, and some protocols have characteristics that are unnecessarily firewall-hostile; and this workshop report. On the working group side, the report suggests charter text in the spirit of protocols developed by a working group being analysed for potential sources of security breach, with identified threats removed from the protocol where possible and documented and guarded against otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: Every RFC should list what could go wrong, say which of those problems the protocol actually fixes, which are fixed elsewhere, and which are not fixed at all, and if the last, say where the protocol must not be used.

sections.title: Core Security Mechanisms
sections.content:
A variety of security mechanisms exist, not all well designed and not all suitable for all purposes. The members of the workshop designated a number of protocols as core, meaning they should be used preferentially if one of them has properties that match the needs of a protocol.

IPsec is the basic host-to-host security mechanism, appropriate for use any time address-based protection would have been used, including with programs such as rsh and rlogin. If and when platforms support user-based keying, that scope may be expanded. One technique used by IPsec, HMAC, is more generally useful: if cryptographic authentication but not secrecy is needed, and IPsec is not applicable, HMAC should be used. ISAKMP/Oakley is the basic key negotiation protocol for IPsec, so it should be deployed when IPsec is used, and with the appropriate domain of interpretation document it should be used to negotiate pairwise keys for other protocols. DNSsec is not only crucial for protecting the DNS, since cache contamination is the easiest way to launch active attacks, but is also needed in many situations when IPsec is used. Security/Multipart is the preferred way to add secured sections to MIME-encapsulated email.

The group also named signed keys in the DNS, noting widespread agreement that DNS records themselves must be protected but less agreement that the key records should be signed themselves, making them in effect certificates, so this is one promising avenue for Internet certificates, and X.509v3 as the other obvious choice for a certificate infrastructure, though again there was no strong consensus. TLS was seen by some as the preferred choice for transport-layer security, though there was no consensus: TLS is less intrusive to the operating system than IPsec, and it is easier to provide fine-grained protection this way.

Some protocols were designated useful but not core, being insufficiently general, too new, or substantially duplicative of core protocols: AFT/SOCKS, RADIUS, firewalls, GSS-API, PGP, Kerberos, PGP-MIME, PKIX-3, the various forms of per-hop authentication such as OSPF, RSVP and RIPv2, POP, OTP, S/MIME, SSH, PFKey, the IPsec API, SASL, and CRAM/CHAP. Entries on that list may move in either direction. A few were considered not useful, primarily because they have failed to catch on even though they have been available for some time: PEM and MOSS. The report adds that this does not imply they are incorrect or lack important information, only that they do not describe protocols the community is currently encouraging the use of.

One mechanism was deemed unacceptable: plaintext passwords. No protocol that relies on passwords sent over unencrypted channels is acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop picked the security tools it thought the Internet should build on, and named the ones it thought were too narrow, too new, or never took off. Sending a password in the clear was ruled out entirely.

sections.title: Missing Pieces
sections.content:
Participants identified three significant missing pieces. Object security means protection for individual data objects, independent of transport. Secure DNS is already one such scheme, but a more general one is needed. MIME is a candidate object framework, in part because it is the core of the two most widely used and deployed applications, the web and email, but securing email has been problematic and the web is not far ahead.

Secure email is a critical need and has been for some time. Two attempts to standardize secure email protocols, PEM and MOSS, failed to be accepted by the community, while a third protocol, PGP, has become a de facto standard around the world. A fourth protocol, an industry standard called S/MIME, has been gaining popularity. Both of the latter entered the Internet standards process.

Route security has recently become a critical need, because the sophistication of the attackers is on the rise and the availability of attacking toolkits has increased the number of sophisticated attacks. The report says this task is especially complex because the requirement for maximum performance conflicts with the goal of adding security, which takes resources that would otherwise improve the performance of the router.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things were still missing: a way to protect an individual piece of data rather than a whole connection, a way to send secure mail that the community would accept, and a way to protect the routing system itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The report says security is not and cannot be a cookie cutter process. There is no magic pixie dust that can be sprinkled over a protocol to make it secure. Each protocol must be analyzed individually to determine what vulnerabilities exist, what risks they may lead to, what palliative measures can be taken, and what the residual risks are.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no shortcut. Each protocol has to be examined on its own to see what can go wrong, what has been done about it, and what risk is left over.

viz.caption: THE PROTOCOLS THE WORKSHOP CALLED CORE

items.title: IPsec
items.text: The basic host-to-host security mechanism, for use where address-based protection would have been used.

items.title: HMAC
items.text: Cryptographic authentication without secrecy, for when IPsec does not apply.

items.title: ISAKMP/Oakley
items.text: The key negotiation protocol for IPsec, and for other protocols with a domain of interpretation.

items.title: DNSsec
items.text: Protects the DNS, where cache contamination is the easiest route to an active attack.

items.title: Security/Multipart
items.text: The preferred way to add secured sections to MIME-encapsulated email.

items.title: Signed keys in the DNS
items.text: Signing key records makes them certificates, one promising avenue for Internet certificates.

items.title: X.509v3
items.text: The other obvious choice for a certificate infrastructure, though there was no strong consensus.

items.title: TLS
items.text: Seen by some as the preferred transport-layer security, being less intrusive than IPsec.

viz.caption: THE THREE PIECES THE WORKSHOP FOUND MISSING

items.title: Object security
items.text: Protection for individual data objects, independent of transport.

items.title: Secure email
items.text: A critical need for some time. PEM and MOSS were not accepted by the community.

items.title: Route security
items.text: Needed because attacks on routing were rising, but it competes with router performance.
